name: Bilal Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a six-person agency on a business park by the ring road, and we do ads for car dealerships, gyms, kitchen fitters, anyone who needs a lot of ads fast. My morning is building the week's ad sets: I feed the offers into two AI tools, get forty versions, throw out thirty, and fix the ten that are close. Afternoons are calls with sales managers who want the price in red and bigger. I like the speed of it. What wears me out is a dealership changing its finance offer at four on a Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does life outside work look, and money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Kasia, my girlfriend, who's a dental nurse. When I was twenty-four my dad helped me buy a one-bed flat, and I rent it out, so that's my real safety net along with about eight months' savings. In the evenings I do freelance ad sets for two car dealers myself, all AI-assisted. My family's big on work and church, and my dad's view is you build something, you don't wait for anyone to hand it to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would surprise me, honestly. I see the tools get better every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who learned the tools still came out ahead, because even small time savings add up. Online I'd probably post a before-and-after of my ad workflow, just to show what a bit of AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a good world for me. I'm faster than the others at Greg's agency because of the tools, so I'm worth more to him, and my freelance work keeps growing. My job's safe and my income goes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, and push the freelance side to four dealers by next summer. I'd put the extra money toward a deposit on a second small flat to rent out. I'd keep using the tools every day, because even a plateau is better than no tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit disappointed, maybe, because I like where the tools were heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the agency would feel the small changes most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Natalia, who does all the resizing and posting. Even small automation eats her day. I've already shown my boss Greg how to batch-resize, so I'm partly the reason Natalia's resizing work is shrinking, and I don't love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything outside AI a worry, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Car dealers are up and down. When interest rates go up, they stop spending on ads, and my freelance work dries up first. But the flat rent covers that, so it's more of an itch than a worry.

say: People who **learned the tools** still came out ahead.
He'd post a **before-and-after** of his ad workflow online.
think: Being faster with tools makes him **worth more** to Greg.
His **freelance work** keeps growing, so income rises.
do: Grow the **freelance side** to four car dealers by next summer.
Save toward a deposit on a **second rental flat**.
Keep using **AI tools** every day at work.
S0.quote: I've already shown my boss Greg how to batch-resize, so I'm partly the reason Natalia's resizing work is shrinking, and I don't love that.
fieldNote: He sees himself as a **winner** from the tools even in a plateau.
He admits his part in squeezing a **colleague's job**.
The **rental flat** cushions the swings of dealership work.

steps.text: Grow freelance ad work to four car dealers by next summer
Save for a deposit on a second one-bed rental flat
Keep running his daily AI ad workflow at Greg's agency

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'm betting on. Honestly it's an opportunity for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market rewards people who move, and I'd tell younger designers to stop complaining and learn the tools. I'd probably post that, and get some angry replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Greg's agency shrinks, but I end up running the ad production while the others go. That's not nice for them. For me, it means more money and maybe a share in the business, or my own small agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd build a full system that turns a dealership's offer sheet into a week of ads with almost no hand work. I'd go to Greg and offer him a deal: I run production, he gives me a cut. If he says no, I'd go out on my own with my four freelance dealers and rent a desk on the same business park.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. I know that sounds bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said that's not nice for the others. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Natalia again, and Marek, who's older and still does everything by hand. Marek's got two kids, so I'd tell my boss Greg to keep Marek on the client side, because Marek's great on the phone with the old-school dealers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would going out on your own cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A desk on the business park is a few hundred a month, the software maybe another hundred and fifty. I'd use two or three months of savings at most to get through the start. The flat rent covers my share of the bills with Kasia anyway.

say: The **market rewards** people who move, and he'd say so openly.
Younger designers should **stop complaining** and learn the AI tools, even if he gets angry replies.
think: Greg's agency shrinks but he ends up **running production**.

do: Build a system that turns **offer sheets into ads** with little hand work.
Offer Greg to run production for a **cut of profits**.
Go **out on his own** with four dealers if Greg says no.
feel: **Calm and excited**, and a bit guilty about it.
S1.quote: Marek's got two kids, so I'd tell my boss Greg to keep Marek on the client side, because Marek's great on the phone with the old-school dealers.
fieldNote: The change **looks good for him**, so he stays calm.
He'd speak up for **Marek**, an older colleague with children.
Going solo would cost **two or three months** of savings at most.

steps.text: Build a system that turns dealer offer sheets into weekly ads
Rent a desk on the business park for his own clients
Ask Greg for a cut of profits in return for running production

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's different. That's not an opportunity, that's the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, same as always, but I'd say it quieter. I wouldn't want to sound like I'm gloating when friends are losing their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I lose the ad business too. If a car dealer can talk to the AI directly and get better ads than me, cheaper, I'm a middleman nobody needs. The robots coming three years later is the window. Anything hands-on still has people in it until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the second flat and keep the cash. I'd talk to my cousin Tomek, who does car wraps and window tints, about buying into his shop, because wrapping a car is hands-on and it's the same dealers I already know. I'd learn to wrap within the first year and bring my clients to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I can feel myself already planning, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Doesn't the wrap shop just buy you three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably. But three years with an income is better than none, and a shop with a unit and machines is worth something when it's sold. After that I don't know. I'd rather be holding property and a business than a design portfolio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kasia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kasia her job is safer than mine for now, because a dental nurse is hands-on. But I'd want us both earning until 2031 and saving hard, and I'd hold off on the wedding we've been talking about.

say: **Adapt** or get **left behind**, but said quietly.
He wouldn't want to sound like he's **gloating** at friends.
think: He'd lose the **ad business** too, as a middleman nobody needs.
The robots' **three-year lag** is the window for hands-on work.
do: Stop the **second flat** purchase and keep the cash.
Buy into cousin Tomek's **car wrap shop** and learn to wrap.
Hold off on the **wedding** with Kasia.
S2.quote: If a car dealer can talk to the AI directly and get better ads than me, cheaper, I'm a middleman nobody needs.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his ad income** but feels in control, so anxious.
His pivot is **hands-on** and uses his existing dealer contacts.
He prefers holding **property and a business** to a design portfolio.

steps.text: Buy into cousin Tomek's car wrap and tint shop
Learn to wrap cars within the first year
Put the wedding with Kasia on hold
Keep the second-flat deposit as cash savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to play it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a five-year sprint and people should use it, not wait for the government to save them. I'd say that at church too, to the younger lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the next three or four years are the best earning years I'll ever have. AI keeps getting better and I'm the one using it best at Greg's agency. Then around 2031 it's over for ad design, so I need to have turned that money into something solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, go out on my own with my dealers and charge per campaign, not per hour. Put most of the profit into the second flat and a stake in Tomek's wrap shop. By year three, I'd want to be working in the shop part-time so the switch isn't a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense. Like before a big match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd charge per campaign rather than per hour. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the AI makes me ten times faster, and charging per hour would punish me for that. A car dealer cares about cars sold, not how long I sat at my desk. Per campaign, I keep the time savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad. He runs a small printing business, flyers and business cards, and he's fifty-eight. I'd want to help him sell it before 2031, while it's still worth something.

He'd tell the **younger lads** at church the same.
think: The next few years are his **best earning years**.

Put profit into a **second flat** and a stake in Tomek's shop.
Work in the **wrap shop** part-time by year three.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way, like before a **big match**.
S3.quote: A car dealer cares about cars sold, not how long I sat at my desk.
fieldNote: His income is **safe for years** and he expects to profit, so uneasy fits.
He worries about his **father's print business** more than himself.
He would **diversify** into property and a hands-on shop early.

steps.text: Go freelance full time and charge car dealers per campaign
Buy a second rental flat and a stake in Tomek's shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's plenty of time to be set up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to be ready with ten years. I'd say families should plan and help each other, and that's what my family would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I come out of this one well. A decade of using AI better than most, building my own agency and two or three rental flats. By 2036 I'd hope to own enough that losing design work isn't the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, keep going at Greg's and keep growing the freelance side. Marry Kasia in the next two years and start a family. By 2030, run my own small agency and own two rental flats, and decide then whether to go into Tomek's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the one that suits how I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the rental flats if lots of people lose work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. Rents could drop if people can't pay. But people still need somewhere to live, and I'd pick rental flats near the hospital, where the hands-on jobs stay longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about work in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn a trade and a bit of business, and to own something, even something small. Owning is what my dad taught me.

say: There's **no excuse** not to be ready with ten years.
Families should plan and **help each other**, as his would.
think: He expects to **come out well** after a decade of using AI better than most.
By **2036** he hopes to own enough that losing design work isn't the end.
do: Marry Kasia and **start a family** within two years.
Run his **own agency** and own two flats by 2030.
Decide in 2030 on joining **Tomek's wrap shop**.
feel: **Calm**, because this scenario suits how he thinks.
S4.quote: I'd pick rental flats near the hospital, where the hands-on jobs stay longest.
fieldNote: He sees **ownership** as the answer, as his father taught him.
He thought through **rent risk** and picked flats near the hospital.
With ten years, the change **looks good** for him overall.

steps.text: Buy a second rental flat near the hospital by 2030
Marry Kasia and start a family within two years
Keep sharpening his AI ad workflow to stay ahead

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Everything I'm good at becomes worthless before I've turned it into something solid. What would help is the government getting out of the way of small businesses, quick permits and low taxes for starting a hands-on business, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to my dad's generation. I'll land on my feet. Men like my dad, fifty-eight with a print shop, are the ones who'll get hit and won't ask anyone for help.

headlineQuote: Men like my dad, fifty-eight with a print shop, are the ones who'll get hit and won't ask anyone for help.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old ad designer** at a six-person agency, using AI tools every day for car dealers and gyms.
He owns a **rental flat**, has eight months saved and runs freelance ad work at night.
He sees slower change as an **opportunity** and stays calm or uneasy while he can profit.
Fast AGI turns him toward **cousin Tomek's wrap shop**, hands-on work with the same dealers.
He believes in **ownership and family** over government help, and worries most about his father.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which makes his skills worthless before he's turned them into assets.
whatWouldHelp: **Quick permits** and low taxes for people starting hands-on businesses, not handouts.
